source.title: Improving Point Cloud Based Place Recognition with Ranking-based Loss and Large Batch Training

record.tranche_reason: The ablation compares batch sizes and reports held-out retrieval performance: the larger batch performs better in both tested architectures, qualifying the claim that large batches hurt under fixed epoch budgets.
record.gate_note: The study reports batch-size comparisons for TruncatedSmoothAP. It does not measure training error or a train-test gap; those parts of V5 are untested. Other versions concern conditions it does not test.
record.test_reason: The study compares batch sizes for point-cloud place retrieval, whereas V5 concerns image classifiers and language models. Retrieval recall under a batch-dependent ranking loss measures a different task; these results do not test any supplied version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the batch-size ablation: TruncatedSmoothAP gives better retrieval recall with batches of 2048 than 256. The broader conclusion is that the enhanced convolutional architecture and training procedure outperform competing place-recognition methods, while the standard benchmarks are approaching saturation.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a point-cloud retrieval task, TruncatedSmoothAP and multistaged backpropagation; it does not compare large and small batches under a standard image-classification or language-model recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size changes reported mean AR@1 for each tested architecture and loss combination.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the Refined protocol with TruncatedSmoothAP, increasing batch size from 256 to 2048 raises mean held-out AR@1 from 96.0% to 97.0% for MinkLoc3D and from 96.7% to 97.9% for MinkLoc3Dv2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger training batches can improve held-out point-cloud place-retrieval recall when using a loss that approximates ranking within each batch.

record.problems: The reported outcome is retrieval recall, not training error or a measured train-test gap. The batch-size comparisons are for one task and one loss; uncertainty estimates are not reported.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results relevant to V5 were left out. The paper's other architecture, loss and state-of-the-art comparisons do not directly test the claim versions.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Held-out performance comparisons between adaptive optimizers and SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Large-batch penalties and their mitigation in image classifiers or language models under fixed epoch budgets.
Effects of adding or removing dropout.
Association between magnitude-aware sharpness and generalization gaps.
Test accuracy after removing highly memorized versus random training examples.

record.verdict_notes: Absence of training-error or train-test-gap measurements is not itself grounds to exclude V5; held-out performance comparisons can test it. The decisive mismatch here is the point-cloud retrieval task. The paper explains that larger batches improve the within-batch approximation of the retrieval ranking objective.

versions.untested_parts: Comparison with fully connected networks or tests isolating local connectivity.
Training error and the train-test gap; language models; fixed-epoch comparisons across workload-dependent batch thresholds; longer training or other adaptation strategies.
Sharpness or other measures of the generalization gap.

rows.subject: MinkLoc3D
rows.operation_detail: Trained with TruncatedSmoothAP at batch size 256; multistaged backpropagation is described for large batches.
rows.note: Table VI reports the mean across evaluation sets; the paper says the 256-element batch result is about 1 p.p. worse than the 2048-element result for this loss.
rows.check: The 96.0% value is correct, but point-cloud retrieval recall does not measure V5. This small-batch comparator alone also cannot establish a partial large-batch penalty.

rows.subject: MinkLoc3D
rows.operation_detail: Trained with TruncatedSmoothAP at batch size 2048.
rows.locator: Ablation study, Table VI; Results and discussion, ablation study
rows.note: The paper states that TruncatedSmoothAP with large batches increases AR@1 of the baseline architecture by 2.5 p.p. to 97.0%; Table VI gives 96.0 at batch size 256.
rows.check: The increase from 96.0% to 97.0% is correct for retrieval recall, but cannot establish reversal of V5 in image classification or language modeling. The separate 2.5-point gain also changes the loss relative to the triplet baseline.

rows.subject: MinkLoc3Dv2
rows.operation_detail: Trained with TruncatedSmoothAP at batch size 256.
rows.note: Table VI reports the mean across evaluation sets; the 256-element batch result is 1.2 p.p. below the 2048-element result for this architecture and loss.
rows.check: The 96.7% value is correct, but point-cloud retrieval recall does not measure V5. This small-batch comparator alone also cannot establish a partial large-batch penalty.

rows.subject: MinkLoc3Dv2
rows.operation_detail: Trained with TruncatedSmoothAP at batch size 2048.
rows.note: The larger batch has higher reported mean AR@1.
rows.check: The increase from 96.7% to 97.9% is correct for retrieval recall, but cannot establish reversal of V5 in image classification or language modeling.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: MinkLoc3D and MinkLoc3Dv2 trained with TruncatedSmoothAP under the Refined protocol
reader_labels.reason: Mean AR@1 is higher at batch size 2048 than at 256 for both architectures (R1–R4), contrary to the stated large-batch penalty.
